Trying linux is not at all hard. You dont even have to touch your windows installation, just to try it.

Go to the linux mint website (more similar to W7 than Ubuntu) and download the .ISO file (I recommend MATE or Cinamon versions), burn that image onto a DVD and reboot your machine from the DVD drive.

This will allow you to try it out without having to install anything on your machine. It will have all the basic software packages, so you will be able to surf the web, try out the office suite, torrent... albeit a bit more slowly than if it was installed on your HDD.

If you later decide to install, it is very simple and painless. You can even browse the web while it installs. Honestly, its less trouble than installing Windows, you wont even have to search for drivers.

It doesn't eliminate Windows unless you wipe the Windows drive/partition to install Mint onto it (which you won't).

You should be able to dual boot (pick the OS at startup), assuming you have sufficient drive space to give Mint its own partition. If you don't have a SSD, you could combine that installation with the extra OS. If you were on a desktop, I'd suggest getting a new small (120gb) SSD just for Mint, since drives are so damn cheap now.

It depends on what you want. The installation wizard gives you options to create partitions. It could cohabitate with Windows, if your disk is appropriately partitioned. In that case, on startup, you would get the GRUB menu, asking what OS you want to boot to.

If you want the two OSes, plan ahead how you want your drive partitioned. If you are just going to have linux installed, its easier, just create 2 partitions on your drive, 1 small system partition and 1 home partition (where your files and user profile will be), that will allow you to upgrade or change linux versions without ever losing your files. You always have the option to go the fully automated route and let the wizard do its thing, it will ask if you want to keep windows or do a clean install of linux. Remember to backup your important data before an installation.

I recommend first trying the live DVD, which gives you the safety of not touching your hard drive, and testing out the system to make sure everything works correctly, you feel comfortable with the OS, etc. No risk involved in that, after a reboot, you will be back to windows.
